sentences.text: Volia is an extinct genus containing only one species, Volia athollandersoni, and belongs to the crocodile family Crocodylidae within the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
The genus name Volia comes from Voli Voli Cave, while the species name honors archaeologist Atholl Anderson.

Its skull featured a snout proportionally deeper than a modern saltwater crocodile that ended abruptly at the tip, along with strongly raised eye sockets connected by a prominent bridge of frontal bone.

Volia possessed large conical teeth with oval bases that became D-shaped at the top due to asymmetrical cutting edges called carinae, giving them a serrated appearance though they were not truly ziphodont like those of Quinkana.

Thirty-five recovered osteoderms of Volia can be classified into five different morphotypes, likely forming armor for the neck and torso that resembled those of modern spectacled caimans and saltwater crocodiles.
Volia was approximately 2 to 3 meters long, making it the largest predator and likely apex predator of Pleistocene Fiji.
Researchers estimated Volia's size by comparing its preserved femur to that of a saltwater crocodile, suggesting it may have reached a length of 2 to 3 meters.
The genus Volia was described by Molnar, Worthy, and Willis in 2002 after fossils were discovered by Trevor Worthy and Atholl Anderson in 1997 and 1998.

Fossils of Volia athollandersoni have been found in the Voli-Voli and Wainibuku caves in the Fiji Islands, with the holotype found in Wainibuku Cave and the largest fossils coming from Voli Voli Cave.

The holotype of Volia is housed at the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa, which also holds the collection of the New Zealand Museum Te Papa Tongarewa containing the holotype of Volia athollandersoni.
Volia likely fed on giant iguanas, flightless birds, or fish, and it is speculated that Volia preyed on iguanas, large birds, or fish during the Pleistocene and possibly Holocene.
Volia may have been more terrestrial than modern crocodiles, and researchers suggest Volia may have been a terrestrial animal, similar to its relative Mekosuchus.
The hinge-like joint motion of the distal ulnare suggests Volia was better adapted to move on land than modern saltwater crocodiles.

Volia lived during the Pleistocene and possibly the Holocene, ranging from the Late Pliocene to the Late Pleistocene, and specifically from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
Volia went extinct around 1000 BC, and fossil material tentatively assigned to Volia from Naigani dates to the Holocene, around 2,900 to 2,700 years ago.
It is debated whether humans caused the extinction of Volia, as remains found in Lapita culture ovens could also belong to modern saltwater crocodiles.
